title: Pentecost: The Spirit Poured Out
summary: On the day of Pentecost the Holy Spirit comes on the gathered believers with the sound of wind and tongues like fire, and they speak in other languages so that pilgrims from across the world hear the wonders of God in their own tongues. Peter explains the event as the fulfillment of Joel's prophecy and preaches that God raised the crucified Jesus and made him Lord and Christ. About three thousand repent and are baptized, and the new community devotes itself to teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayer.
story: Jesus told his followers to wait in Jerusalem for the promised Spirit (1:4-5), and they have been praying together. Now the promise arrives. This chapter is the launch of the church's witness in Jerusalem, the first stage of the program in 1:8. It also looks back across the whole Old Testament. Moses wished that all the LORD's people were prophets and that he would put his Spirit on them (Numbers 11:29); Joel promised exactly that for the last days; and the confusion of languages at Babel (Genesis 11) is answered by a gift in which people of many languages hear one message. The chapter ends with a portrait of the first church that Luke will return to again and again.
historical:
Pentecost, from the Greek for fiftieth, was the Jewish Feast of Weeks (Shavuot), held fifty days after Passover to celebrate the wheat harvest (Leviticus 23:15-21; Deuteronomy 16:9-12). It was one of three pilgrimage festivals when Jewish men were expected to come to Jerusalem, so the city was crowded with visitors. In later Jewish tradition the feast was also associated with the giving of the law at Sinai; how early that association was made is debated, but if it was current, the coming of the Spirit on this day would carry added meaning.

The list of peoples in verses 9 to 11 sweeps roughly from east to west, from Parthia and Media beyond the Roman Empire's eastern frontier through Mesopotamia and Asia Minor to Egypt, Libya, Rome, Crete, and Arabia. It represents the Jewish Diaspora, the communities of Jews living outside the land of Israel, some of whom had settled in Jerusalem and others who had come for the feast. Converts to Judaism (proselytes) are included. The third hour (verse 15) was about nine in the morning. Peter's point is that it is far too early for a festival crowd to be drunk.
cultural:
Wind and fire were familiar signs of God's presence in Israel's Scriptures: the burning bush, the pillar of fire, the fire and smoke on Sinai, and the wind or breath of God (the same word as spirit in both Hebrew and Greek). John the Baptist had promised that Jesus would baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire (Luke 3:16). The first readers would recognize that God himself had come.

Galileans had a recognizable accent (compare Matthew 26:73), so the crowd's amazement that Galileans were speaking the languages of distant lands is natural. Peter's sermon relies on Jewish ways of reading Scripture: David was regarded as a prophet, and his psalms were read as speaking of the Messiah, the anointed king God had promised from David's line. David's tomb was known in Jerusalem in Peter's day, and Peter uses that fact to argue that Psalm 16 cannot be about David himself, since David's body did see decay. The common meals, shared goods, and daily temple worship of verses 42 to 47 show believers who are still fully Jewish in practice, meeting in the temple courts and in homes.
literary: The chapter has three parts: the event (1-13), Peter's explanation (14-41), and a summary of the community's life (42-47). Peter's speech is the first full sermon in Acts and sets a pattern for others: it starts from what the listeners have just seen, quotes Scripture, tells the story of Jesus' life, death, and resurrection, appeals to the apostles as witnesses, and calls for a response. It builds on three Old Testament passages, Joel 2:28-32, Psalm 16:8-11, and Psalm 110:1, and it climaxes in verse 36, where the crucified Jesus is declared both Lord and Christ. Luke often sums up the growth and life of the church in short summary passages like verses 42 to 47, which serve as pauses in the narrative.

outline.t: The Spirit comes with wind, fire, and tongues
The crowd hears in its own languages
Peter explains: this is what Joel foretold
Repent and be baptized; three thousand added
The life of the first community

doctrines.note: The Spirit is poured out on all people, men and women, young and old, servants included, as Joel promised. The Spirit's first work is to enable witness to the wonders of God. The exalted Jesus is the one who pours out the Spirit (2:33), so the Spirit's coming is itself evidence that Jesus reigns.

Joel's promise, “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved,” is applied by Peter to calling on Jesus. The response he asks for is repentance and baptism in Jesus' name for the forgiveness of sins, with the promise of the Spirit. How baptism relates to forgiveness is debated (see the hard question), but the gift is plainly offered to all whom God calls, far and near.

The first church is marked by four practices: the apostles' teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayer. Its members share their possessions with anyone in need, worship with gladness, and grow as the Lord adds to their number. Luke presents this as the fruit of the Spirit's coming, not a program the apostles designed.
Jesus was handed over by God's set plan and foreknowledge, yet those who crucified him are responsible. Peter holds God's purpose and human guilt together without explaining how they fit.

words.note: Glossa, tongue, meaning either the physical tongue or a language. In verse 3 it describes the tongues like flames; in verses 4 and 11 it means languages. At Pentecost the hearers recognize their own native languages, which most interpreters take as speaking real human languages not learned by the speakers. Whether the tongues-speaking described in 1 Corinthians 12 to 14, which required interpretation, is the same gift or a different form of it is debated.

Ekcheo, to pour out. Joel's prophecy speaks of God pouring out his Spirit, and Peter says the exalted Jesus has poured out what the crowd now sees and hears (2:33). The image is of abundance: the Spirit is not rationed to prophets, kings, and priests as in the Old Testament but lavished on all God's people.

Metanoeo, to repent, literally to change one's mind, but in biblical use a turning of the whole person from sin to God. The Hebrew idea behind it is turning or returning. Peter calls a crowd implicated in Jesus' death to turn and be baptized, and the same call to repentance runs through the preaching of Acts.

Koinonia, fellowship, participation, or sharing. It describes life held in common, and verse 44 shows its practical form: believers had everything in common (koina, a related word). The word is used elsewhere for sharing in Christ, in the Spirit, and in the Lord's Supper, and for financial gifts between churches.

christ: Peter's sermon is the first public announcement of who Jesus is after the resurrection. Jesus of Nazareth, a man certified by God through miracles, was crucified according to God's plan, but death could not hold him. God raised him, as David foresaw, exalted him to his right hand, and made him both Lord and Christ. The title Lord here applies to Jesus the name that Joel used for God himself, since those who call on the name of the Lord are saved by calling on Jesus. The outpoured Spirit is the evidence of his enthronement. The chapter shows that Jesus is not merely a remembered teacher but the reigning Messiah who gives God's own Spirit to his people.

hard.q: What does Acts 2 teach about speaking in tongues, baptism, and receiving the Spirit, and must every believer's experience follow this pattern?
hard.a:
Christians read this chapter in several ways. Pentecostal and many charismatic Christians see Pentecost as the pattern of a baptism in the Spirit that may follow conversion as a distinct experience of empowering, and classical Pentecostal teaching holds that speaking in tongues is its initial evidence. Many Reformed, Baptist, and other evangelical Christians see Pentecost as a unique, once-for-all event in the history of salvation, like the cross and resurrection, marking the Spirit's arrival for the church; on this view every believer receives the Spirit at conversion and tongues are not required. Among those, some believe the miraculous gifts continued (continuationists) and others that they ceased with the apostles (cessationists).

On baptism, Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, and some other Christians read verse 38 as teaching that God grants forgiveness and the Spirit through baptism. Baptists and many evangelicals hold that forgiveness comes through repentance and faith, with baptism as the commanded public sign that follows. Those who baptize infants often point to the promise to you and your children (2:39); those who baptize only believers note that it continues to all whom the Lord will call, and that verse 41 says those who received the word were baptized. These are second-order questions on which faithful churches differ. All agree that the Spirit is the gift of the risen Christ, that repentance, faith, and baptism belong together in the New Testament, and that the Spirit is promised to all who belong to him.

questions: At Pentecost people heard the gospel in their own languages. What does it suggest about God that he did not require everyone to learn one sacred language first?
Peter tells the crowd, God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ. Why do you think the crowd was cut to the heart rather than simply offended?
Look at the four practices of verse 42. Which of them is strongest and which is weakest in your own life or church, and why?
